carrosseis.titulo: Trotsky’s lover ended up painting the man who had him killed.
carrosseis.legenda:
Trotsky’s lover ended up painting the man who had him killed.

The story the university leaves off the feminist T-shirt.

At the university, Frida Kahlo is a “feminist icon.” Her life has chapters the print does not show. With dates:

• January 1937: Trotsky, exiled by Stalin, arrives in Mexico. Diego Rivera, Frida’s husband, secures the asylum, and the couple house him at the Blue House, in Coyoacán, with his wife, Natalia Sedova.
• 1937: Frida and Trotsky have an affair, under her husband’s roof, with Natalia in the house. The affair is over by July. On 7 November 1937, Frida gives Trotsky Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky.
• 1939: Rivera breaks with Trotsky, who leaves the Blue House.
• 20 August 1940: the Soviet agent Ramón Mercader attacks Trotsky in Coyoacán. He dies on the 21st.
• c. 1954: Frida, by then a Stalinist, paints Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick and Frida and Stalin. She dies on 13 July 1954.

The argument: Trotsky was killed in 1940 by an agent of Stalin’s secret police, on Stalin’s orders. In 1954, Frida painted Frida and Stalin, a portrait of devotion to the dictator. So Trotsky’s former lover ended up honoring the man who had him killed.

The T-shirt chooses the chapter. The whole story is in the dates.

Save this for when someone admires Frida, and send it to them.

#FridaKahlo #Trotsky #History

Sources:
- Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (1983).
- Pavel Sudoplatov, Special Tasks (Little, Brown, 1994), pp. 69 and 71, on the operation against Trotsky.
- Isaac Deutscher, The Prophet Outcast: Trotsky, 1929-1940.
- Frida Kahlo, Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky (1937), National Museum of Women in the Arts.
- Entries “Frida Kahlo” and “Leon Trotsky” (Wikipedia), checked on 7 October 2026.

carrosseis.titulo: Doctor: a boy raised as a girl, and it worked. In 2004, at 38, he killed himself.
carrosseis.legenda:
Doctor: a boy raised as a girl, and it worked. In 2004, at 38, he killed himself.

Bruce (later David) Reimer was born on 22 August 1965, in Canada, twin of Brian. In 1966 a botched circumcision destroyed his penis. The parents saw the sexologist John Money on television and took the boy to Johns Hopkins, in Baltimore. Money argued that boy or girl identity came from upbringing. At 22 months David was castrated and raised as “Brenda,” with dresses and hormones. Brian was the control.

In 1975 Money published the case as “Ablatio penis: normal male infant sex-reassigned as a girl,” and presented it as a success. At 14, the boy refused a girl’s identity, was told the truth, and chose the name David.

In 1997 Milton Diamond and Keith Sigmundson published the follow-up: David had never accepted being a girl. Brian died in 2002. David killed himself on 4 May 2004.

If sex were only upbringing, David would have accepted himself as a girl. He did not. So the case Money called a success shows the opposite.

Sources:
John Money, “Ablatio penis: normal male infant sex-reassigned as a girl,” Archives of Sexual Behavior (1975).
Milton Diamond and H. Keith Sigmundson, “Sex reassignment at birth: long-term review and clinical implications,” Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine (1997).
John Colapinto, As Nature Made Him (2000), for the later history up to that date. The death on 4 May 2004 is from contemporary reports of that year (and later accounts by Colapinto).

carrosseis.titulo: Picasso, the Communist Party painter, died a millionaire. His grandson drank bleach.
carrosseis.legenda:
Picasso, the Communist Party painter, died a millionaire. His grandson drank bleach.

Pablo Picasso died on 8 April 1973, at 91. A member of the French Communist Party from 1944, designer of the dove for the World Peace Congress (1949) and winner of the Lenin Peace Prize (1962), he left about 45,000 works and no will.

His grandson Pablito, 24, son of Paulo, the painter's first son, was refused entry, with Marina, when Picasso died. After that refusal he drank bleach (The New York Times, 17 April 1973). He was already in hospital on the funeral day, and died three months later. Marina wrote in 2001 that they grew up with little money and were often turned away at the gate of villa La Californie, in Cannes.

The obvious objection: Paulo was an adult, the widow barred him, and Marina is an interested party. But Paulo was chauffeur to his millionaire father, and the grandchildren's poverty lasted for decades while the grandfather lived.

The argument:
• Anyone who lends his name to the party of the poor, and leaves his own grandson in poverty when he could have lifted him out of it, denies at home what he signs on the poster.
• Picasso, a PCF member and a millionaire, left his grandchildren to grow up with little money (Marina Picasso, 2001).
• So Picasso denied at home what he signed on the poster.

Which counts for more: the dove on the poster, or the grandson at the gate?

Sources:
• Marina Picasso, Picasso, mon grand-père (Denoël, 2001); English, Picasso: My Grandfather, trans. Catherine Temerson (Riverhead, 2001).
• The New York Times, "Picasso Buried in a Private Rite," 17 April 1973.
• About 45,000 works and a six-year partition, settled in 1979, are standard in English estate reporting.

Images: Wikimedia Commons. Chapelle Notre-Dame-de-Vie de Mougins, Berdea (CC BY-SA 3.0); "20220503 141620 Villa La Californie," Indigo&fushia (CC BY-SA 4.0); "Pablo picasso 1," Vea y Lea (public domain); others in the public domain.

carrosseis.titulo: Whoever drives God out of society ends up worshipping a dictator. T. S. Eliot warned in 1939.
carrosseis.legenda:
Whoever drives God out of society ends up worshipping a dictator. T. S. Eliot warned in 1939.

Eliot, later the 1948 Nobel laureate in Literature, gave three lectures at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, in March 1939. Faber published them in October as The Idea of a Christian Society. He said the essay was not meant as an anti-communist or anti-fascist manifesto.

He did not trust a hollow democracy: “The term ‘democracy’ does not contain enough positive content to stand alone against the forces that you dislike; it can easily be transformed by them.” And the line that made the carousel travel: “If you will not have God (and He is a jealous God) you should pay your respects to Hitler or Stalin.”

The first premise comes from a secular sociologist. In The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), Émile Durkheim wrote that a society cannot go on forever in the void left when the old gods grow old or die. In 1793, Paris raised an altar to Reason. When a society becomes enthusiastic about a man, Durkheim wrote, that man will be, as it were, deified. He died in 1917. He was describing the mechanism, not Hitler or Stalin.

In 1948, in Notes Towards the Definition of Culture, Eliot wrote that no culture has appeared or developed except together with a religion.

Sources:
T. S. Eliot, The Idea of a Christian Society (Faber and Faber, first edition, October 1939), pp. 13, 57 and 63.
T. S. Eliot, Notes Towards the Definition of Culture (1948), p. 13 (introduction).
Émile Durkheim, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, trans. Joseph Ward Swain (Allen & Unwin, 1915), pp. 213-214 (Book II, ch. VII; the “old gods” sentence is in the conclusion). French original 1912.

carrosseis.titulo: You cannot understand the left without this word: infantilization.
carrosseis.legenda:
You cannot understand the left without this word: infantilization.

Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., a forensic psychiatrist who evaluated defendants for the courts, writes in The Liberal Mind (2006): Rossiter's point, in The Liberal Mind, is that as governments become more actively custodial, the governed become more passive and dependent. Custodial means treating the adult as a child.

The state, he says, is “a proper source from which to gratify the longings of the people for various forms of parental care.” And: “The modern state has taken on the role of an apparently benign, generous, omnipotent and god-like parent, who serves as custodian, manager, provider and caretaker, all to the detriment of the people.” In his account, “We have, in effect, parentified our governments.”

Under modern liberalism, the citizen “is not called to maturity but is instead invited to begin a second childhood.” The usual excuse is to blame “society.” Rossiter answers: “A competent individual always remains a unique and lifelong cause of his own experience.”

On character: “They do not feel entitled to be subsidized by persons with whom they have no prior personal relationship or contractual duty.”

No one learns to do what someone else always does for him. To keep an adult unable to do what is his to do is to infantilize him. The left calls it progress to hand the state, as a permanent right, what belongs to the adult. So that idea of progress infantilizes the adult. If you miss this, you do not understand the left.

I read this book 10 years ago, before it became fashionable.

Sources:
Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., The Liberal Mind: The Psychological Causes of Political Madness (2006). English wording from the author’s excerpts at libertymind.com. The custodial-governments sentence matches the Portuguese edition photographed for this series (Vide, 2016, p. 47).

Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II.

carrosseis.titulo: The left has a psychiatric report. The diagnosis: madness. Lyle Rossiter, a forensic psychiatrist, gave his book the subtitle “The Psychological Causes of Political Madness.”
carrosseis.legenda:
The left has a psychiatric report. The diagnosis: madness. Lyle Rossiter, a forensic psychiatrist, gave his book the subtitle “The Psychological Causes of Political Madness.”

He describes how a self-governing adult is formed. Under modern liberalism, he writes, the citizen “is not called to maturity but is instead invited to begin a second childhood.” The modern state has taken on the role of a “god-like parent.”

Among the early foundations he lists are tolerance for frustration, a reduction of infantile dependence, and the loss of the child’s sense that the world exists to serve him. Without an early limit, he argues, the urge to dominate overpowers respect for the sovereignty of others.

An honest warning: the book does not say that every spoiled child becomes a militant. It shows the mechanism. Those excused from effort are left without the virtues of self-reliance and self-control.

The argument: to demand that someone else provide what you can obtain by your own effort is the spoiled child’s conduct. The state produces nothing: what it gives, it first took from those who work. An able adult who asks the state for what he could earn acts like a spoiled child, with the state in the parents’ place.

I read this book 10 years ago, before it became fashionable.

Sources:
Lyle H. Rossiter Jr., The Liberal Mind: The Psychological Causes of Political Madness (2006). Author biography at libertymind.com: more than 2,700 civil and criminal cases. English wording from the author’s excerpts at libertymind.com (On the Ideals and Dangers of Liberalism; On the Appeal of Modern Liberalism). Lists from the early-childhood chapters are given as paraphrase; the English pages were not confirmed in a citable official source. Aristotle is in the background of the Portuguese series, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II.

carrosseis.titulo: The heir of the Frankfurt School admitted: human rights are a Jewish-Christian inheritance.
carrosseis.legenda:
The heir of the Frankfurt School admitted: human rights are a Jewish-Christian inheritance.

“To this day, there is no alternative to it,” Jürgen Habermas said in 1999, in a conversation with Eduardo Mendieta. Habermas (1929-2026) was the leading name of the second generation of the Frankfurt School.

The sentence, in English, is this: “Egalitarian universalism, from which sprang the ideas of freedom and social solidarity, of an autonomous conduct of life and emancipation, of the individual morality of conscience, human rights and democracy, is the direct heir to the Judaic ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love.” He adds that, to this day, there is no alternative to that legacy, and that “everything else is just idle postmodern talk.”

He was speaking of historical origin, not calling for conversion. That is already enough to drop the myth that human rights were born against the biblical inheritance.

John Lennox, emeritus professor of mathematics at Oxford, quotes the same admission when answering the new atheists.

Sources:
Jürgen Habermas, "A Conversation About God and the World," interview by Eduardo Mendieta, 1999, in Time of Transitions (Polity, 2006), pp. 150-151.
Jürgen Habermas, "Religion in the Public Sphere," Holberg Prize lecture, 29 November 2005 (later, European Journal of Philosophy 14, 2006): "key resources for the creation of meaning and identity."
John Lennox, Gunning for God (English page not confirmed; the Portuguese Em Defesa de Deus cites p. 77, not transferred).
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, article 1, for "equal in dignity and rights."

carrosseis.titulo: Plato wrote that tyranny is born only from democracy.
carrosseis.legenda:
Plato wrote that tyranny is born only from democracy.

In Republic VIII, in Paul Shorey's translation (Plato in Twelve Volumes, Harvard / Heinemann, 1969), democracy falls by the good it pursues: a hunger for freedom, when the city is "intoxicated by drinking too deep of that unmixed wine" (562d). At 564a: "tyranny develops out of no other constitution than democracy: from the height of liberty, I take it, the fiercest extreme of servitude." The tyrant "sprouts from a protectorate root and from nothing else" (565d), after the demos puts forward "one man as its special champion and protector" (565c). In the early days he smiles, swears he is not a tyrant, cancels debts and divides land. Then he invents some war, so that the people will need a chief.

Aristotle, his pupil, checks it against history. In Politics 1310b, trans. H. Rackham (Harvard / Heinemann, 1944): "almost the greatest number of tyrants have risen, it may be said, from being demagogues, having won the people's confidence by slandering the notables." In old times, "whenever the same man became both leader of the people and general, they used to change the constitution to a tyranny" (1305a).

A conservative mistrusts the man who grows by accusing the notables and asking for power in the people's name.

Sources:
Plato, Republic VIII, 562b-d, 564a, 565c-566e, trans. Paul Shorey, Loeb, 1969.
Aristotle, Politics V, 1305a and 1310b, trans. H. Rackham, Loeb, 1944.
